nameStory: The 'flying' in northern flying squirrel is actually a bit misleading – these little acrobats don't truly fly like birds or bats! Instead, they glide through the forest canopy using a furry membrane stretched between their front and back legs, like a living parachute. The 'northern' part of their name distinguishes them from their smaller southern cousins who prefer warmer climates.
description: Northern flying squirrels are enchanting nocturnal mammals about the size of a hamster, growing 10-15 inches long including their flattened tail. They have soft, silky fur that's light brown on top with pale, creamy underparts. What makes them truly special is the stretchy skin membrane called a patagium that connects their front and back legs, allowing them to glide gracefully between trees in the darkness. Despite their aerial skills, they're surprisingly clumsy when walking on the ground.

idTips.label: Gliding Membrane
idTips.description: Look for the loose, furry skin flap connecting front and back legs – it's visible even when not stretched out for gliding, giving them a distinctly 'baggy' appearance along their sides

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: About hamster-sized at 10-15 inches long with a notably flattened, furry tail that acts like a rudder during glides – much flatter than a regular squirrel's bushy tail

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Incredibly soft, dense fur that feels almost velvety to the touch – light brown to grayish-brown above with creamy white or pale gray belly fur

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Strictly nocturnal and rarely seen on the ground where they move awkwardly; listen for soft chittering calls and watch for gliding silhouettes between trees at night

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for small gnaw marks on tree bark, tiny pellet-like droppings near tree cavities, and collections of lichen or soft material that they use for nesting

habitat: Northern flying squirrels prefer mature coniferous and mixed forests with plenty of tall trees for gliding, especially areas with spruce, fir, and hemlock. They need forests with tree cavities for nesting and an abundance of lichens and fungi, which make up much of their diet. In New England, look for them in higher elevation forests and areas with dense canopy cover.

seasonality.spring: Breeding season begins and females may be found in tree cavities with young. Fresh gnaw marks on maple trees appear as they tap into spring sap flows.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for foraging, with peak gliding activity on warm, calm nights. Young begin learning to glide and may be spotted making short, clumsy practice flights.
seasonality.fall: Intense foraging as they cache fungi, nuts, and lichens for winter. Multiple individuals may begin sharing winter nest sites during cold snaps.
seasonality.winter: Several flying squirrels often huddle together in shared tree cavity nests for warmth. Activity decreases but they don't hibernate, emerging on milder nights to feed on cached food.

funFact: Northern flying squirrels are living glow sticks! Their belly fur glows bright pink under ultraviolet light, and scientists still don't fully understand why – it might help them communicate with each other in the dark forest or could be related to their diet of fluorescent lichens and fungi.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with their smaller cousin, the southern flying squirrel, which is more common in New England. Northern flying squirrels are noticeably larger, have grayer-brown fur (vs. more reddish-brown), and the hair on their belly is gray at the base with white tips, while southern flying squirrels have all-white belly hair from base to tip.
contextualKnowledge: Don't expect to see flying squirrels during daytime nature walks – they're among the most strictly nocturnal mammals in New England. Many people live their entire lives in flying squirrel habitat without ever knowing these magical gliders are there, since they're active only in complete darkness and are naturally secretive.
compareHints: Northern flying squirrels are significantly larger than southern flying squirrels and prefer cooler, higher elevation coniferous forests rather than the mixed hardwood forests favored by their southern relatives. The northern species has grayer fur and a more robust build, while southern flying squirrels are smaller, more reddish, and found in warmer climates. Both have the distinctive gliding membrane, but northerns are better adapted for cold weather with denser fur.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Southern flying squirrels are smaller and grayer than their northern flying squirrel relatives, with less contrast between their back and belly colors.
